refuted.why:
Drove the file in Playwright. One sub-claim reproduces; the two costs it is built on are factually wrong, and the fix would make the file worse.

WHAT IS TRUE: focusing [data-act="group-about"] and pressing ArrowDown does move focus to .idxRow and announce "2 of 14. Mara & Finn's menu tasting...". notebook.js:1457-1462 confirms the binding is global whenever `typing` is false.

COST 1 — "keyboard page scrolling is dead everywhere outside a field" — FALSE. There is no page scroll to kill. At 1440x960 in ?state=pressure (36 notes, 900-word note) document.scrollingElement is 960/960; with a note open it is still 960. The single scrollable region in the whole file is #index (1497/267, 1497/579 with a note open). In that region the arrow handler is not stealing the reading gesture, it IS the reading gesture: focusing the first row and pressing ArrowDown twelve times walked the cursor and carried the scroller 0 -> 240. And PageDown is not bound at all: from a focused .idxRow, PageDown moved #index 0 -> 233. So the "one gesture a person uses to read a long pile" both works and is served better than the finding's fix would serve it.

COST 2 — "a segmented control cannot be walked with the arrows a person will reach for" — the demonstration does not match the claim. The arrows a person reaches for on a horizontal two-segment switch are Left/Right, and Left/Right are unbound: I focused group-day, pressed ArrowRight, and focus stayed on group-day. Nothing is hijacked from the keys the control's own pattern claims. The control is `role="group"` + two `aria-pressed` toggle buttons (notebook.js:676-679), both tab stops, both named, both announcing pressed state — a valid APG toggle-button-group, not a broken radiogroup. Swapping it to role="radiogroup"/role="radio" with roving tabindex is a lateral pattern preference (and arguably wrong semantics: this is a mode toggle, not a form choice), i.e. taste stated as a defect.

WHAT REMAINS is a deliberate global list-navigation model: Up/Down/j/k always belong to the pile, exactly as they do in Linear, Gmail and Superhuman. The move is non-destructive, announced in the live region, and recovered with one ArrowUp or Shift+Tab. Nothing is changed, nothing is lost.

THE FIX WOULD REGRESS TWO THINGS. (a) Scoping to activeElement.closest('#index') kills the walk from the opened-note desk: after clicking a row, focus sits on "Put it back" (data-act="close"), outside #index, and ArrowDown currently advances the index cursor there. Reading is the product's core loop; the fix makes you Tab back into the index between every note. (b) Deleting the bare "/" branch removes the universal search convention. The "/" behaviour is also already reasoned in-source (notebook.js:1358-1362): the caret starts in the capture field by design, so from the resting state "/" is a character — I pressed it and got "/" in .topField, state still notebook, which is correct for a capture product — and Ctrl+K is the advertised chord precisely because the file cannot honour "/" from the state it opens in. That "/" additionally works when not typing is a bonus, not a broken advertisement; and after "/" from an open note, two Escapes return cleanly to notebook.

refuted.problem: The chip is the boldest object in the resting frame and its accessible name promises "Go through them". Clicking it announces "8 notes to decide." and does nothing else. Nothing else in the master opens the hand either — the dock carries Search, Dictate, Read a photo and Account, the head carries the chip, the privacy control and options. The review hand exists only at ?state=review, so the product's decision engine, the thing the chip is counting, has no entry point a person could find. A control whose label names an action it does not perform is worse than no control: a stranger presses it, hears nothing, and concludes the count is decoration. Then, once inside the hand, the remaining count is stated four ways on one screen in four grammars — "2 of 8" on the card, a dash rail top right, "7 still to decide" in the ledger line, "6 left" on the pile header — three different numbers within 350px of each other, all of them correct and none of them reconcilable at a glance.

Factually wrong about the behaviour, verified by driving the file. The secondary count claim is also mis-stated. refuted.problem: The designer's notes to the panel are set in the product's own type slots, inside the sheet, addressed to a reviewer. Your note stayed here." A screen-reader user is the only person told the product is a mock.

Every quoted string is accurate, but the argument fails on three of its four locations and its fix would make the artifact worse.

2. The say() charge is factually wrong in its strongest sentence. 3. Both branches of the proposed fix are worse than what is there. The structural half of the fix — "a fixed lab gutter outside the white paper" — puts a fourth persistent element on the ink floor, which is the locked frame (ink floor, one sheet, capsule spine left, dock at the foot). Residue, recorded but not sufficient to carry the finding: the pressure room is the one place where lab wording is grafted onto a genuinely product string rather than sitting in acknowledged apparatus — "THE PILE" and "36 notes" are identical to the notebook room, and "peak season, an extension of the fixture" is appended to them. That is one clause, in one lab-only room, seen by no customer. It is a register nit, not the systemic "design marking its own homework in the customer's voice" the finding argues, and it does not justify the redesign proposed.

REFUTED on both halves; the coordinates are right and the story attached to them is wrong.

2. The kbd claim is wrong about the source. master.css:782, inside `@media (pointer: coarse)`, already contains `.undoAct kbd { display: none; }`. The proposed fix is strictly worse than what ships: keying the kbd off `!phone.matches` swaps input modality for viewport width, so a touch laptop or an iPad at 768+ would start printing a chord it has no keyboard for, and a narrow desktop window would lose a chord it does have. The CSS already solves it the right way.

3. The residual occlusion is not a checklist violation. `.undo` is a 10-second self-dismissing `role="status"` toast (notebook.js:126), and the pile already carries a floor for it: `.index` padding-bottom 148px on phone fully clears the strip — scrolled to the very bottom at 390, `coveredAtBottom` is empty. Linear, Things and Stripe all float undo over the list; none of them reflow it.

4. The primary proposed fix would make the work worse. A laid-out band between `.indexHead` and `.index` shoves the entire pile down ~46px the instant a note arrives and yanks it back up 10 seconds later — two unrequested layout jumps bracketing the most frequent act in the product, fighting the scroll and focus place-keeping the 171-assertion gate exists to guard. The alternative (conditional `scroll-padding-bottom` plus a matching pad "for as long as it is present") resizes the scroll container mid-toast for the same jump, and buys nothing at scrollTop 0, which is exactly where the user is after every keep.

refuted.problem: Measured at 1440: the sheet is 1322px and a note being read is 512px, hugging the left edge with 810px of nothing beside it, while the index rows immediately below run the full 1214px. Two planes on the same white sheet disagree about the page's width by a factor of 2.4, so the desk reads as a phone layout inflated onto a desktop rather than a composition. The same hole sits beside the peel, the hand, the readback and every empty state. iA Writer and Bear hold the same measure and centre it; Things gives the column a counterweight. Here the right two-thirds of the most important surface in the product is dead air, and it is the thing that most undercuts the otherwise expensive first impression.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Measured live at 1440 in Chromium across notebook/capture/readback/review/seam/pressure/nothing/not-yet.

1. It is wrong about two of the four elements it names. `.handCard` is 183–1339 (1156px, 87% of the sheet) with its 8-tick progress bar pinned to the card's right edge and its foot running "Decide later · Delete · Back to the pile Esc" out to that same edge; only the three-line `.handBody` sits at measure. That is precisely the counterweight the finding asks for, already built. `.emptyBody` (496px) is a hero headline on a full-width card sitting directly on top of a full-width two-column grid of four empties — a left-aligned hero over a filled grid is Stripe/Linear-standard composition, not a hole. Neither surface shows what is described.

2. `.peel` is 720px because the locked architecture says the seam "peels a second, SMALLER piece of paper off the note." Widening it or standing a column beside it contradicts a locked element.

3. The numbers are wrong in ways that carry the argument. `.readBody` is 527, not 512. The index rows are 1262, not 1214 — 1214 is `.topFoot`, which is inside the paper. The space right of the text within the paper is 711px, not 810px, and it is bracketed above by `.readSrc` (1214px, full paper width) and below by `.topFoot` (1214px) whose primary action lands on the paper's right edge in every single state. The paper asserts its own full width top and bottom in the index's own grammar; the finding measures only the middle band and reports it as the whole plane.

4. The comparison is not like for like. A paragraph held at 68 characters versus a one-line index row carrying title + preview + state + timestamp are different content types with different correct widths, sitting on two planes the locked architecture separates by depth. "The page disagrees with itself by 2.4x" is a ratio between a paragraph and a table row, not a defect about one object.

5. Both proposed fixes make it worse or break the lock. Centring the column breaks the single left leading edge — paper content at 154, `.readSrc` at 154, `.topFoot` at 154 — and would produce dead air on BOTH sides of a 1262px paper instead of one, while orphaning the column from the index below. Bear does not centre (its editor is left-aligned; its panes eat the width); iA Writer centres because it has no index beneath. The second-column fix imports an inspector rail into the desk and moves the seam action off the peel, which is a redesign of locked elements and out of scope.

The grain of truth is one state, not four: at `pressure` a 150-word note leaves a genuine 711 x 560 void mid-paper. That is worth a narrow finding; this one is not.

refuted.problem: Opening any note removes the capture field from the document entirely — `.topField` count is 0 — and focus lands on "Put it back". I typed "a thought while reading": activeElement was BODY and every character was discarded with no ink, no field, no announcement. Reading is not an edge state here, it is the second half of the locked architecture, and in it the product's whole promise is off the screen. The only way back is a 36px unlabelled glyph in the dock (aria-label "Write a note", no visible text) that a venue owner has no reason to read as "start a new note". Linear, Things and Bear all keep the capture affordance alive while you are reading; this one silently swallows keystrokes at the exact moment a thought arrives.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven in Playwright at 1440x960, both by deep link (?state=notebook&open=n02) and by the real path (Tab to the index, Enter on a row; also click). The one measurable half of the claim is true and trivial: readSheet() replaces topSheet(), so `.topField` count is 0 while a note is on the desk. Everything the finding builds on top of that is wrong or already answered.

1. "The only way back is a 36px unlabelled glyph in the dock" is false. On the real path, focus after opening lands on `[data-act="close"]`, a visible-text button reading "Put it back" with a visible `Esc` kbd hint (measured 130px wide), and Escape restores the desk and the capture field (fields 0 to 1, live region "Put back."). That is two advertised routes back before the dock glyph is reached; the glyph is the third.

2. The reproduction conflates two runs. "activeElement was BODY" only happens on the deep link, where the boot seeds the caret with `mount.querySelector(".topField, .phoneField")` and there is no field to seed. Open a note the way a person does and activeElement is the labelled "Put it back" control. "No announcement" is also wrong: opening announces politely, measured as "Open. Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn."

3. Already deliberately handled, and the source says so at notebook.js:415-421: "On a wide screen the capture field is on the desk's paper, and reading a note replaces it. So the dock carries the way back to writing, which is otherwise off the screen entirely." And where capture matters most, it is never lost at all: at 390x844 with a note open, `.phoneField` count is 1 and the note is open at the same time. The desktop read state is the only place the field steps aside, which is exactly the locked architecture ("the desk carrying the newest piece of paper, which is where you write... Reading lifts a note out of the index onto the desk").

4. The benchmark argument cuts the other way. Linear, Things and Bear keep a persistent new-item control in the chrome; they do not keep a live text field on top of the thing you are reading. This file keeps exactly that persistent control in the dock. Typing prose into Linear with an issue open also produces nothing.

5. Both proposed fixes are worse. (a) A permanent capture strip under every read note turns the locked two-plane desk into a standing three-surface desk; the peel precedent is a transient sequence, not a resting fixture. (b) Type-to-capture collides with the file's own bare-key model, measured live: with a note open, "j" keeps the note open and walks the index cursor with an announcement ("2 of 14. Mara & Finn's menu tasting..."), and "/" opens search. Seeding a draft from any printable key swallows both, or needs a carve-out list that reintroduces the "advertised but not implemented" hazard the programme already paid for.

Residual grain, too small to be this finding: after Escape the caret lands on the index row rather than the capture field, so the next character still goes nowhere. That is the programme's own focus place-keeping guard working as designed (return focus to the control you came from), and changing it would break the index arrow walk continuity. Also, with focus on "Put it back", a space inside typed prose activates the button and closes the note; that is standard button behaviour, not a defect.

rounds.headline: The floor rose to 6.1 and the ceiling to 7.4, and all seven seats named one distance. The subject axis answered the structural charge in the group headers and nowhere below them: the desk was a generic composer, the row was a workflow-status table, and every note a person actually wrote was filed silently under one default. As the taste seat put it, the domain lived in about eight percent of the pixels. And the phone row fix recorded last round had never rendered — it was aimed at a different file and failed silently, so five separate seats measured the same defect twice.
rounds.body: Twenty-six findings confirmed, nine refuted. The subject is now something the product does rather than something the fixture carries: the capture sheet says where the words will go, opening on what the venue is facing; a note can be re-filed from the note itself; the rule that heads a group leads rather than trails; the grouping survives thirty-six notes; and the whole axis is a real heading on the accessibility tree, where it had resolved to nothing at all. The two planes share one column at every width, the peel is a smaller piece of paper again, and one object sits at the foot of a phone rather than two.

wins.biggestWin: Put both planes on one content column. Add `--stack: min(100%, 1040px)` and apply it to the desk paper, the hand card, the peel and the index wrapper, keeping `--measure` as an inner cap on the writing lines only. That single change closes the 546px-to-1056px void beside the desk, stops the index preview from running at a 210-character measure at 1920, pulls the orphaned status and time columns back to within 24px of the sentence they annotate, gives the dock a centre to belong to, and turns the two objects into the stacked planes the architecture describes. Every other finding here is smaller and partly downstream of it. On the standing structural charge: the subject grouping is real and it is venue-shaped — grouping by couple and dating against the event rather than the typing day is a genuine answer, not a relabel. But it answers only in the group headers. The desk is still a generic composer and the row's right side is still a workflow-status table, so at 1920 the pile reads as a project tracker with wedding words in it. That is a taste problem I will let the taste seat price; the composition problem above is mine, and it is the one keeping this off a 9.

Apply one rule everywhere the product shows a person's words next to a machine's version of them: the person's words are always the largest, densest type in the pair, and they always get the line before the metadata does. That is a single principle with three edits — raise .saidWas to 17px at full ink over the standard 31em measure, raise .peelFrom span to match .peelField exactly, and rebuild the phone row so .idxText takes the full width over two lines with the chip and timestamp demoted to a 12px ink-3 second line. Those three edits fix the two most costly findings at once and they are the difference between a well-made notes app and one that means its own promise. On the structural charge, plainly: the subject grouping is answered in the data and the copy and is not yet answered in the type — it is set 13 per cent smaller than the rows it heads, in the same weight and colour, and it is switched off entirely at 36 notes. Fix the type on it and the charge is closed; leave it and the answer stays invisible at a glance, which is the only place it was ever meant to work.

Make the subject-grouped pile the pile in every state that lists notes, not just the resting one. Concretely: delete `noDays: true` from STATES.pressure and from STATES.review's empty branch, make .idxDay sticky inside #index, give the phone row two lines so the subject survives at 390, and rewrite the loading line to promise that order instead of "newest first". Right now the answer to round 2's structural charge exists in one state out of ten and disappears the moment there are 36 notes — which is the only condition under which a venue operator in peak season ever sees this product. Carrying it everywhere is what turns "we rebuilt the pile" from a claim about the demo into a claim about the product, and it is a handful of lines because the machinery already exists.

Make "what it is about" something the product does rather than something the fixture carries. Right now every note a person writes is hardcoded into "The house" and there is no control anywhere to set, change or create a subject — so the pile's structure is a rendering of pre-tagged seed data, and swapping the fixture for pre-tagged engineering standups would change nothing on screen. Add a subject chip to the capture field (defaulting to the venue's own next date, N.next) that writes into makeNote's `about`, make the subject segment on the read sheet a button that reopens the same picker, and land the newly captured note where the eye already is. That single change converts the structural answer from a display into a product, fixes the misfiling, and repairs the capture moment the whole thing is sold on — it is worth more than the other four findings combined.

Lock the lexicon and make the product speak one language. Today the same place has four names (the pile, the hand, Notes, here), the same event has six (turn, turned, send, sent, crossed, has it), undo announces the sentence it just reversed, and four strings the product actually ships were thrown away and rewritten — one of them into a claim about offline behaviour that contradicts what notes-copy.ts says the product does. Fix it as one change: two nouns and one verb ("your notes", "still to decide", "send"), applied to every eyebrow, button, tag, section and live region; the undo template inverted so Ctrl+Z says "Put back. Nothing crossed into Tasks."; and privacyLong, emptyBody, voiceStop and offline restored verbatim with a gate that fails on any unused copy key. That single pass repairs the copy contract, the reversibility announcement and the vocabulary in one edit. On the structural charge: the subject pile does answer it — a notebook that opens on "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 to decide" is not a standup list, and it was rebuilt rather than re-labelled. But the answer stops at the data. "Mara & Finn, in 2 days" is set in the same weight, the same ink and the same size as "The studio · No date", so the product knows a wedding is bearing down on this woman and then renders that knowledge at the volume of everything else. That, not any of the five defects, is the distance to 9.5: it knows what the notes are about and declines to act like it.

Rebuild the phone, starting with the index row. This is not an even product: the 1440 resting state genuinely looks like a top studio's shipped work and a stranger would pay for it, but at 390 — the surface a venue operator actually holds while walking a car park — the pile is fourteen unreadable 13-character stubs, the dock and capsule never merged, and the note you just captured lands underneath the dock. Fixing the row grid alone (restack to two lines, metadata to a quiet second line) converts the phone from a demo into the product and takes the score past 8.

On the structural charge: it is answered at the level of the organising principle and unanswered at the level of every individual object. The subject grouping is real, not re-labelled — "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 to decide" is a wedding, a date and a pressure count in one line, and ordering a wedding in two days above a college reading due today is a domain judgement no generic notes app makes. The readback state is the memorable moment and it is genuinely of this world: one spoken breath becomes two separable notes with "2 notes, not one" and an X on each, because people walking a site talk in run-ons. That is a product idea, not a feature. But strip the group headers and what remains — the desk, the row, the peel — is entirely generic. The domain lives in about 8% of the pixels. So: not "an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words", but a well-made notes app with a genuinely wedding-shaped spine and wedding-blind furniture hanging off it. Make one object below the header know what it is about — the row, the desk, or the peel — and the charge closes for good.

Make the note a person just wrote the first thing in the pile, and give them a way to say what it is about. One change fixes three separate failures: the words currently fly to a row that is below the fold at 1280x720 and 1024x768, the just-captured note is filed ninth under a subject nobody chose, and the subject axis is decoration the product cannot generate. Pin session-captured notes to a band above the first subject rule (labelled with the product's own \"Just now\"), scroll the index to the arriving row before flyWords starts, and put a subject picker in the capture sheet's foot feeding makeNote. Do that and the three-second promise ends where the eye already is, and the structural answer stops being a property of the fixture.

confirmed.element: .top / .behind / .handTop / .handCard { max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 220px) } (master.css:275) against .index / .idxRow, which are fluid to the sheet
confirmed.problem: The desk plane is frozen at 716px from 1100px upward while the index plane grows with the window. Measured left/right edges: at 1280 the paper is 130→846 and the row is 120→1242; at 1440, 130→846 against 120→1402; at 1920, 130→846 against 120→1882. So the newest piece of paper occupies 56% of the sheet at 1440 and 40% at 1920, and a dead white field 546px wide (1440) to 1056px wide (1920) sits to its right in every state, in all four rooms, containing nothing at any width. The two planes share no right edge, no measure and no scaling rule, so they do not read as a desk above an index; they read as a card sitting on an unrelated table. The architecture says reading lifts a note out of the index onto the desk, and the geometry says the opposite: the lifted note is 44% narrower than the row it came from. The CSS comment at line 269 shows the last round diagnosed this exact relationship and treated one side of it by shrinking the paper, which moved the imbalance rather than resolving it. The composition is only correct at one viewport: at 768 the paper is 110→734 and the row 100→744, sharing a right edge, and that frame is the best-composed image in the set.
confirmed.fix: Do not widen the paper. Make the index resolve to the paper's own column, and give the surplus to the ink floor rather than to the sheet. Three moves: (1) add `--plane: calc(var(--measure) + 220px)` to :root and replace line 275 with `max-width: var(--plane)`, so the frozen number becomes a named token both planes can read; (2) cap the index to the same column — `.indexHead, .index > *` (or a wrapper inside `.index`) `{ max-width: var(--plane) }` — so `.idxRow`'s 20px/1fr/76px/92px grid resolves against the paper's width and the row's content edges land on 130 and 846 at every viewport, exactly as they already do at 768; the row trims are word-safe and re-run on resize, so the shorter excerpt costs nothing but a few characters. (3) Cap the sheet so the leftover is ink, not white: `.sheet { max-width: calc(var(--plane) + var(--gutter) * 2); margin: 0 auto }` under a min-width guard, letting the ink floor absorb everything past ~776px of content. The result is one left rail at 130, one right edge at 846, one measure, and one scaling rule across both planes at every width; the 768 relationship becomes the rule; the growing white void disappears into the floor the architecture already owns; and the paper keeps the width line 269 argued for. Verify by re-measuring `.top` and `.idxRow` right edges at 768/1100/1280/1440/1920 and asserting they agree within the row's 10px negative margin — that assertion belongs in notes-audit.mjs as a tenth check.
confirmed.done: One --stack token, and both planes resolve to the same content column at every width. The desk was frozen at 716px from 1100 upward while the index grew with the window, so the two objects the architecture calls stacked planes shared neither edge and a void sat beside the paper. Three gate assertions measure the two edges at 1280, 1440 and 1920.

confirmed.element: .idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px minmax(0,1fr) 76px 92px; column-gap: 13px } (master.css:414), unoverridden inside @media (max-width: 720px)
confirmed.problem: The desktop four-column grid survives verbatim onto a 360px row. Measured at 390: the person's words get 113px, the status chip and the timestamp get 76 + 92 plus three 13px gaps, so 168px of hard-reserved metadata beats 113px of writing. The words are then truncated twice, by the file's word-safe JS trim and again by `text-overflow: ellipsis`, so the rendered row reads 'Saturday wed…', 'Mara & Finn's …', 'Ask the venue …', 'Idea for the st…'. Five consecutive rows are indistinguishable on the surface a venue operator actually holds mid-shift, while 'In Tasks' and '35 minutes ago' are fully legible. Round 2 recorded this as fixed — that the phone row gives its width to the person's words over two lines with the facts on a quiet second line. That change is not in the built file; there is no .idxRow rule anywhere under 720px.
confirmed.fix: Two corrections to the proposed fix, then it is right. (1) The proposal puts .idxTag and .idxWhen both in grid-column 2, which stacks them into two separate lines. Give the phone row three columns so the caption is one quiet line: in the 720 block, `.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px max-content minmax(0,1fr); column-gap: 10px; row-gap: 3px; align-items: start; padding: 10px }` `.idxText { grid-column: 2 / -1; grid-row: 1; white-space: normal; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: clip; display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; line-clamp: 2; -webkit-box-orient: vertical }` `.idxTag { grid-row: 2; grid-column: 2; justify-self: start; font-size: var(--t-11); font-weight: 400; color: var(--ink-3); box-shadow: none; padding: 0 }` `.idxWhen { grid-row: 2; grid-column: 3; justify-self: start }`. Dropping the pill's ring and its 600 weight on the phone is the other half of the fix — a two-line row that still carries a ringed bold pill has only moved the tax, not paid it. State survives as ink density (To decide keeps the dot on .idxMark i, which is already there) and the accessible name is untouched, so nothing is lost to a screen reader. (2) Do not merely early-return from trimRows() below 720. The function rebuilds innerHTML from data-full at the top of each iteration, so a bare return would leave a desktop-width trim frozen in the DOM after a resize down, and the interaction gate's resize assertion would pass on a stale string. Guard it as: if readWidth() is true, restore `lede rest` in full, delete dataset.clipped, and return — so crossing the breakpoint in either direction hands the clamp the whole sentence and it truncates exactly once.
confirmed.done: The desktop four-column grid no longer survives onto a 360px row. The words take the row over two lines; the state and the time take a quiet second line under them. Assertions measure the share of the row the words get, the number of lines, and the characters that survive.

confirmed.element: .peel { max-width: min(720px, calc(100% - 40px)); margin: 9px 6px 0 34px } (master.css:627) against .top at 716px
confirmed.problem: The locked architecture calls the peel a second, smaller piece of paper off the note. Measured in ?state=seam it is 720×373 hanging off a note that is 716×162 — 4px wider and 2.3x taller than its parent, and in ?state=review after T it is 720×417 under a 716px hand card. The subordinate object carries more than twice the visual mass of the object it was torn from, so the eye lands on the peel first and the note reads as its caption. Its edges resolve to nothing: inset 34px from the note's left, overhanging 38px past the note's right, so neither side aligns and the overhang is what signals 'bigger'.
confirmed.fix: Replace master.css:627 `max-width: min(720px, calc(100% - 40px)); margin: 9px 6px 0 34px` with `max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 120px); margin: 9px 0 0 24px`, and add the comment the geometry is missing: the peel is capped 100px inside the note's own `--measure + 220px` cap so it is smaller by declaration, not by accident. Verified at 1440: peel becomes 616 wide at x 154–770 — its left edge lands exactly on the note's 154px text rail, its right edge sits 76px inside the note's right edge, height unchanged at 373px, action row still one line. At 768 it resolves flush with the note's right edge (734) instead of the current 6px near-miss. Keep `.peel::before { left: 30px }` so the notch still points back at the tear, and leave the max-width:720px media override (`.peel { margin-left: 12px; margin-right: 0 }`, line 844) as is. If the panel wants the mass ratio addressed as well, that is a separate and harder question about the peel's content, not its box.
confirmed.done: The peel is a smaller piece of paper again: narrower than the note it came from, with its own padding cut back. It was four pixels wider and 2.3 times the area.

confirmed.element: .idxRow at 390 wide — master.css phone media block; round 2 claimed two lines for the words with the facts on a quiet second line
confirmed.problem: The phone row does not do what the programme says it does. Driven at 390x844 the row is 40px tall and .idxText renders on exactly one line (measured lines: 1), trimmed to "Mara & Finn's menu…" — 18 characters of a 70-plus-character note — while an "In Tasks" chip and "2 hours ago" hold the right third of a 390px screen. On the device where capture actually happens, the person's own words lose two thirds of the row to metadata that is identical on nine rows out of ten. The pile becomes a column of ellipses; nothing can be recognised without opening it, which turns every glance into a navigation.
confirmed.fix:
Take the proposed @media (max-width: 720px) rebuild as written — grid-template-areas "mark text" / ". facts", row-gap 5px, align-items start, .idxText at white-space: normal with -webkit-line-clamp: 2, and an .idxFacts flex line carrying the chip and the timestamp at --t-12 — with four amendments the finding does not cover:

1. trimRows() (notebook.js:499-527) measures scrollWidth vs clientWidth. Once .idxText is white-space: normal the condition at line 507 is false on the first pass, so the whole word-safe trim silently becomes a no-op and the browser's own clamp does the cutting, which breaks at the character and can slice mid-word — the exact damage the comment at line 522 was written to prevent. Give trimRows a phone branch that measures scrollHeight > clientHeight instead and pops whole words against the two-line box, keeping the four-word floor and the data-clipped backstop.

2. Do not flatten the chip to a uniform box-shadow: none; font-weight: 400. Today .idxTag[data-quiet] (Kept) is distinguished from the ringed states (To decide, In Tasks) by ink density, which is how this palette is allowed to carry state. Drop the ring on the facts line if you like the quieter result, but keep the distinction by alpha — ringed states at --ink-2, data-quiet at --ink-3 — or the phone loses a state distinction the desktop row makes.

3. The row grows from 39.9px to roughly 66px, so re-check .index { padding-bottom: 148px } against the merged dock and the @media (pointer: coarse) row padding at master.css:866, and re-run trimRows after the reflow rather than before it.

4. Gate it where the gate is blind. Add to the 390x844 block in notes-interaction-check.mjs: (a) every visible .idxText renders two lines or its full text, i.e. clientHeight >= 2 * line-height when data-full is longer than what fits one line; (b) every row shows at least 40 characters or its complete text; (c) the .idxText box is wider than the combined facts line. Without (b) this regresses the moment anyone touches the media block again — which is what appears to have happened between round 2 and round 3.
confirmed.done: Same fix. -webkit-box could not do it: a grid item's display is blockified, so the clamp was discarded and the row collapsed back to one line. Two leadings of max-height does the same job and survives being a grid item.

confirmed.element: .topField 1.55 / .readBody 1.62 / .handBody 1.58 / .readLong 1.66 / .piece 1.52 / .peelSent 1.45
confirmed.problem: Measured on the same sentence driven through the product: 17px/400 at 26.35px leading in the field you type it in, 27.54px when you open it on the desk, 26.86px in the hand, 28.22px when the note is long, 25.84px in a readback card. Tracking splits too — 17px carries -0.021em on the desk and the field, -0.016em in .piece, .peelSent, .peelField and .emptyBody. The declared three-step ladder (--lh-tight / --lh-base / --lh-read) governs the chrome and is overridden by a literal on every single surface that carries a person's writing, so the ladder is real for labels and fictional for content. The consequence is concrete: type six lines, press Ctrl+Enter, open the note again, and the block is 7px taller than the one you wrote. The gate only forbids line-height: normal, so it does not see this. iA Writer's whole discipline is that the words do not move.
confirmed.fix: Add one token, `--lh-note: 1.62`, beside the other three, and one honest note in the comment that content leading is a fourth step because content is not chrome. Replace the literal with `line-height: var(--lh-note)` on `.topField` (317), `.readBody` (367), `.handBody` (576), `.piece` (541), `.emptyBody` (674), and change `.topField { min-height: calc(1.55em * 2) }` to `calc(1.62em * 2)`. Unify tracking at 17px on `--tr-18` for every one of those rules plus `.peelField` (637) and `.peelSent` (649); leave those two at 1.45, they are single-line titles. Do not flatten `.readLong` to 1.62 as filed — a 900-word note earning more air is a real craft move, so keep it as a declared second token (`--lh-long: 1.66`) rather than a naked literal, and accept that a note crossing the long threshold re-leads once on open. Then fix the half the finding missed: `[data-type="expressive"] .topField` (784) sets 20px with no leading and no tracking, so it inherits the 17px literal and the 17px token while `.readBody` (781) gets 1.6 and `--tr-21`. Give the expressive field the same leading and tracking as the expressive read view, or the same words rewrap between the field they were typed in and the desk they are read on. While there, `[data-type="expressive"] .readLong` at 17px inside an otherwise-20px read view means a long note is a different SIZE than a short one in studio and press — decide that deliberately. For the gate, do not whitelist four ratios globally: `.darkSaid` 1.38, `.emptyTitle` 1.22, `.saidWas`/`.peelWhy`/`.specWhy`/`.state p` 1.55, `.darkNote` 1.6 and the 390 field's 1.5 would all fail, and forcing display type onto a body ladder makes the work worse. REFUTED on three independent grounds, each measured live at 1440x960.

Landing at 154 would require col + gap = 24 total, i.e. a 20px icon with a 4px gap to the text, which no benchmark named here would ship, or moving the paper's inner padding to 33px, or breaking the sheet gutter. That is an invisible-affordance regression of exactly the kind the standing checklist names, and it grows the receipt from 111px to roughly 170px, pushing both pieces and the "Put both on the pile" commit down a 960px viewport. (2) `.peelFrom span` at 17px/600 becomes byte-identical in type to `.peelField`, so the static quote and the textarea a venue owner must find and edit read as the same object inside a 720px panel.

CONSTRAINT. The fix explicitly proposes to "let the tint carry the difference". The locked constraint is that state is ink DENSITY and FILL, never colour — density is the sanctioned mechanism and it is what is carrying the distinction today. The fix removes it and leans on background tint alone.

The closing law — "nothing derived may be larger or denser than the words it came from" — is already violated by the file's own correct behaviour: `.pick` (source, 17/400) and `.peelField` (derived, 17/600) sit at the same size, and that is right, because one is a quotation and one is an editable field. This is taste asserted as law, with the strongest counter-evidence (34px `.darkSaid`, 17px `.pick`) unlooked-at.

refuted.problem: Four uppercase 11px/0.075em labels of three different structural ranks are rendered identically in one view: a card title (TURN THIS INTO A TASK), two field labels (THE WORDS YOU PICKED, THE TASK WORDING) and a sheet section header (WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS). Caps stop signalling rank once they answer every labelling problem, and the seam is the flow where rank matters most. In the same card 13px runs at three trackings and two leadings — .act and .picker at -0.156px, .peelBoundary at -0.13px, .peelWhy at -0.078px, at 1.45 and 1.55 — because `--tr-13` is never declared and three rules silently fall back to a literal `-0.01em`. The stated "one tracking curve, by size, declared once" is not true of the file. And .peelBoundary, the boundary promise that opens the peel, is the one paragraph in the product without `text-wrap: pretty`, so it breaks as "the exact words you / pick and check below".
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The observations are partly true but every operative part of the fix fails measurement, and two of its factual premises are wrong.

TRUE: --tr-13 is undeclared (master.css:95-97), three rules use var(--tr-13, -0.01em) (392, 597, 605), and line 93 claims every letter-spacing is a token. Seam does render four identical 11px/0.825px/600/ink-3 caps labels.

1) THE TRACKING HALF IS A NO-OP. Declaring --tr-13: -0.010em and replacing the three call sites changes zero rendered pixels; the fallback already resolves to exactly that. Measured trackings at 13px in seam: .act/.picker -0.156px, .peelBoundary -0.13px, .peelWhy -0.078px. The widest gap is 0.078px per character, ~4.7px over a 60-char line, ~0.026px between the two the fix actually touches. Sub-pixel per glyph. This is a comment that overclaims, not a design defect at 9.5.

2) .topMeta IS 12px, NOT 13px. Computed in all four rooms: 12px / -0.072px. The fix instructs "change .peelWhy and .topMeta from var(--tr-12) to var(--tr-13) so 13px has one tracking" — that puts a 12px element on a 13px tracking and breaks the exact "one curve, by size" rule the finding invokes.

3) text-wrap: pretty ON .peelBoundary IS DEMONSTRABLY INERT. Applied live and re-measured line rects via Range.getClientRects(): before [384,128], with pretty [384,128]. Identical. The fix does not fix the break it names. (balance yields [264,249], but balance was not proposed.) The break is also not a defect: 384/128 of a 403px measure is a 32% second line, not a runt.

4) "THE ONE PARAGRAPH WITHOUT text-wrap: pretty" IS FALSE. .stays ("Your note is still here, still private, still yours") wraps to two lines in the same card with no pretty. Multiple other prose runs likewise.

5) THE CAPS FIX CONTRADICTS ITSELF AND MAKES THE WORK WORSE. It leaves .indexHead ("WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS") untouched, so the seam still shows two caps labels, not "the only caps label in the seam" as claimed. And the proposed replacement register — 12px / 400 / --ink-3 / no caps — is already the file's register for quiet facts (.topMeta, .pickCount, .stays, .idxDayTail, .indexHead .cnt). Demoting a field label into it removes the one cue separating a label from the 15px ink-1 content directly beneath it, trading a rank collision among labels for a rank collision between label and fact. Caps census across all ten states also shows seam is not the densest: ?state=nothing renders five (4x .specName + .indexHead), unaddressed.

Residue worth one line, not a finding: .peelBoundary (lh 1.45) and .peelWhy (lh 1.55) are two 13px paragraphs in one card at two leadings.

refuted.problem: The product's whole promise is the three seconds between a thought and it being safe, and the moment ends badly. Ctrl+Enter empties the field, and the flying-words layer carries the sentence 670px down the sheet to row 10 of 15, at the very bottom edge of the visible index, under a heading called "The house" that has nothing to do with what was written. At the resting 1440x960 it is on the last visible line; at any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen. The head count ticks 14→15 and the chip ticks 8→9, so the only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header — not the words themselves.
refuted.why:
Driven in Playwright at 1440x960 against notebook.html, the finding's two load-bearing claims are false and its fix would break a tested contract.

(1) "At any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen." Measured the opposite. Eight successive Ctrl+Enter captures, pile growing 15 -> 22 rows: the arriving row's position is i=9 on the first keep, then i=4 (top:594, bottom:634) on every keep after, never clipped by #index, never off viewport, always ~250px clear of the dock. The reason is in the source I read: groupsOf() breaks ties between no-date groups with `bag.get(b).length - bag.get(a).length`, so as "The house" accumulates the new notes that group climbs the order. Growth makes the landing more visible, not less. The escalation the finding rests on does not exist.

(2) "The only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header." False on four counts, all measured: #say announces "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision."; the undo strip reads "Kept on the pile. / Undo Ctrl+Z"; the row carries data-arriving with a 620ms arrive animation; and the flying words land on a row that IS on screen — rowT 837.5, rowB 877.4, dock top 878, elementFromPoint at the landing point returns .idxRow, unobstructed. The words are the confirmation, and they are visible.

The one accurate observation — the first keep lands the row on the last line above the dock — is a one-off caused by initial group sizes and self-corrects on the very next capture.

(3) The fix would make it worse. `scrollIntoView({block:"center"})` after every keep moves the pile under the reader on every single capture. Place-keeping across repaint is an explicit contract here: paint() captures and restores #index.scrollTop by design, with the rule stated in the source comment ("Nothing here may cost the operator their place"), and notes-interaction-check.mjs asserts it at lines 93-121. Yanking the pile to centre on each keep is the opposite posture from Things or Bear, where capture never disturbs where you are reading. The pinned "Just now" duplicate row is worse still: it prints a row under a heading that contradicts the grouping the round-3 charge is being judged on.

Residual worth noting but not this finding: if the reader has scrolled the pile down first, the restored scrollTop leaves the arriving row ABOVE the visible index (measured rowT 43 against idxT 303) and the ghost flies up into the desk. That is real, narrow, and the exact inverse of what this finding describes, so it cannot be confirmed as written.

refuted.problem: Four notes-copy.ts strings are never rendered and have been replaced by strings this master wrote: voiceStop ("Stop listening" → "Stop and read it back"), emptyBody ("The capture field is ready above." → "Nobody else can read what you write here…"), privacyLong ("Yours until you send something on" → "Nobody else can read this"), and offline. The offline substitution is not a rewrite, it is a different product: notes-copy says "Reconnect and try again" (the person retries) and the card says "Notes will put it on the pile the moment you reconnect" (it happens by itself). One of those two sentences is a lie to a venue manager whose note is sitting on a phone in a field. Grep confirms copy.privacyLong, copy.emptyBody, copy.voiceStop and copy.offline each have zero call sites.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The grep is right and the argument built on it is wrong; three of the four sub-claims are factually mistaken about which slot the notes-copy string belongs to, and the proposed fix would put two false sentences on screen.

1. OFFLINE — the headline claim, and it is wrong. `offline: "You are offline. Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again."` lives in notes-copy.ts `errors` (notes-copy.ts:218), the hand-off error set, documented alongside `tasksUnavailable`, `replyLost`, `retryPending`, `sourceChanged`. It is the error for trying to SEND A NOTE TO TASKS while offline. notes-copy.ts has a separate `destination.offline` ("You are offline. Your note stays private here.") and no key at all for a note captured offline. notebook.js:1216 is not that fact: the card is headed "Held on this device", the desk above it reads "Written while the connection was down", and the state describes a note that was WRITTEN offline and is waiting to sync. Two different facts, not two grammars for one. There is no lie and no contradiction. Applying the fix would print "Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again" on a card about a locally held note, i.e. it would tell the venue manager in the field to retry a Tasks send she never started, and would delete the one sentence that answers her actual question (does it sync by itself). The fix makes the product less honest, not more.

2. EMPTYBODY — the fix would state something false about the screen. I drove ?state=nothing at 1440x960: STATES.nothing replaces the top sheet's textarea entirely (notebook.js:1145-1155, no `topField`), so the rendered page is title, body, then two first-move buttons — there is no capture field above the body. On a phone capture is in the dock, below. Rendering "The capture field is ready above." verbatim would point at a field that is not there, and would trade two working first moves ("Write the first one", "Or say it") for a pointer, which is the standing checklist's own "empty states that repeat themselves instead of offering one first move".

3. PRIVACYLONG — no such key exists in notes-copy.ts. data.js invented the name for `capture.headerAssurance` ("Yours until you send something on"), a HEADER string. notebook.js:658 is the capture foot, whose notes-copy counterpart is `capture.privacyAssurance` ("Private until you send it on"). The finding is asking for a header string to be rendered in the capture slot, which is itself the placement change the fixture's own comment permits ("a direction may only decide where a string lives"). Also note data.js's `privacy: "Private to you"` is already not verbatim from notes-copy either, so the "verbatim fixture" premise the finding rests on does not hold at the source it cites.

4. VOICESTOP — the only sub-claim with force: "Stop listening" became "Stop and read it back" at :1024. It is a real deviation and it is two words. On a full-floor takeover the primary action naming its own consequence, where the next state is literally "What you said, once", is what Things and Linear do. The finding itself offers to withdraw it ("put 'and read it back' nowhere"), which is taste conceded as taste. Not a defect at 9.5.

5. THE GATE IS WRONG. data.js is a shared fixture read by render-a.js, render-b.js, render-c.js and notebook.js. I checked all four: none of them render voiceStop, emptyBody, privacyLong or offline. The fixture is a menu of the product's strings, not a manifest of one direction's screen. A gate that fails on any unused key would force copy into slots whose fact it does not state — exactly the three errors above — and would break the three sibling directions too.

refuted.problem: Every undo announces the past-tense sentence for the action it just reversed. Driven live: Ctrl+Z after a keep says "Undone. Kept on the pile."; after a send it says "Undone. Sent to Tasks." A person who is not looking at the screen hears the product confirm the exact thing they just cancelled. Reversibility is this product's safety claim and its announcement states the opposite of what happened.
refuted.why:
The quoted behaviour is accurate — I drove it and got `say="Undone. Kept on the pile."` after Ctrl+Z on a keep and `say="Undone. Kept in Notes."` after undoing K in the hand (notebook.js:144). But the reading of it is wrong and the proposed fix would make the product worse.

WRONG ABOUT THE BEHAVIOUR. "Reversibility ... its announcement states the opposite of what happened" mis-parses the sentence. The head of the utterance is "Undone."; the label is its object. A polite live region is spoken start to finish in order, so there is no moment at which "Kept on the pile" stands alone in the ear. Naming the reversed act is information, not contradiction: it identifies WHICH of several stacked acts came back, which is precisely what an eyes-off operator needs after the ten-second strip has timed out. This is the standard undo grammar shipped by every benchmark named in the brief and by the OS itself ("Undo Typing", "Undo Move"). It is not a defect that undo names its object.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE — three ways, all verifiable in the file:
1. "Put back." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for closing an open note (notebook.js:468). Reusing it as the undo stem gives one sentence two meanings, breaking the "one noun for one fact" rule this programme just paid to establish.
2. "Nothing was kept." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for discarding dictation (lines 1448, 1494, 1590, 1596). Saying it after undoing a keep is worse than ambiguous: I confirmed that undo restores the words live into the capture field (`field="Ring the florist about the arch"`, caret returned). Telling a venue owner "Nothing was kept" at the exact instant her words are sitting safe in the field reads as loss. That is the one failure this product cannot afford, and the fix introduces it.
3. "Tasks did not receive it." asserts a fact about another product's internal state that Notes cannot observe. The sealed one-way edge means Notes knows only that it did not send; claiming Tasks did not receive is an unverifiable outward promise.

ALREADY-CONSIDERED. The label string is shared deliberately between the pre-undo strip and the post-undo announcement, and the code comments at notebook.js:186 and :417 record that a previous round shipped the post-undo phrasing on the pre-undo strip and had to reverse it because it told the operator their note had gone back to the sheet while it was safely on the pile. The finding proposes re-splitting that seam with the strings that caused the earlier failure.

refuted.problem: Computed over every element in the resting 1440 view, indigo appears exactly twice: the wordmark dot and an 8% tint on whichever row the cursor is on. The one fact only this product has — that this note's words have already crossed a sealed one-way edge — is rendered in the same greyscale pill as "To decide" and "Kept". The accent is being spent on a browser state and withheld from the product's second promise, which is obeying three colours rather than spending them.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the count is wrong, and the element it missed is the one that kills the argument. Computed over every element in the resting locked 1440 view, indigo appears three times, not twice: the rail mark dot (5x5 at 58,57), the cursor row's 8% tint, and — by far the largest indigo object on the page — a solid rgb(79,70,229) 1px ring around the entire 716x151 capture sheet (master.css:287, `.top:has(.topField:focus-visible)`), plainly visible in locked-notebook--1440x960.png. The accent is not "spent on a browser state"; it is spent on the product's first promise, drawn around the place a thought goes in three seconds. master.css:20 states that rule explicitly: "the one indigo — the live edge of whatever you are doing right now."

The pill claim is also wrong. "Kept" is not the same pill: it renders `data-quiet` (master.css:443) with no outline, ink-3, weight 400, and reads as unpilled in the frame. "In Tasks" and "To decide" share the outline, but pending rows carry the filled ink dot on their own mark (notebook.js:794, `.idxMark i`), which master.css:19 declares as the "waiting on you" signal and master.css:20 pairs with "in Tasks — an outlined chip, ink at full strength". Both states also differ in the accessible name (notebook.js:779). The selector cited, `.idxRow[aria-current]`, does not exist; it is `[data-cursor]`.

The crossing is already indigo, exactly where it is live: `.pick` on the picked words, `.pickBar` hairline, `.peelFrom` on the words printed above the wording they became, and `.readBody::selection` (master.css:587–625). Indigo means the crossing as it happens. The fix asks it to also mean a settled historical fact on every past row, which is the opposite reading of the same colour on the same screen.

The fix would make it worse twice over. At rest 3 of 14 rows carry "In Tasks", so three indigo pills would sit in the pile competing with the desk ring and the cursor; in the "What has crossed into Tasks" ledger every row is crossed and its tag is the lane name (notebook.js:781), so the proposed rule would not even reach the one surface the finding cares about. And taking the cursor row to "ink 4%" lands it on `--wash` (rgba(17,17,17,0.035)), which already carries both `.idxRow:hover` and `.idxRow[data-open]` — collapsing three distinct states onto one fill and regressing the gated single-tab-stop arrow walk so a keyboard cursor becomes indistinguishable from a hovered row.

refuted.problem: The desk column runs 130 to 846 (716px). The index rows directly beneath it run 120 to 1402 (1282px). That leaves 556px — 43% of the sheet — of permanently empty white to the right of every desk object, in every state and in all four finished rooms. The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge while the rows below go to the sheet wall. The two planes do not read as depth, they read as an unfinished right half with a full-bleed list under it. A discerning stranger looking at a 1440 screenshot sees a layout that ran out.
refuted.why:
The geometry is right and everything else about the finding is wrong. Measured at 1440x960: `.top` 130–846 (716px), `.paperStack` 130–1392, `.idxRow` 120–1402 (1282px). So the 556px band exists. But:

1. THE FIX RE-CREATES THE DEFECT ROUND 2 REMOVED, AND I PROVED IT. I applied the exact proposed fix in Playwright (`.top,.behind,.handTop,.handCard{max-width:980px}` + `margin-inline:auto` on `.paperStack`) and re-measured. `.top` becomes 980px (130–1110) — and the content does not move: `.topField` stays 154–681 (527px) and the 900-word `.readBody` in ?state=pressure stays 154–681. Every text-bearing rule on the desk is capped at `--measure` (31em) independently of the paper. So the fix does not remove 264px of white, it relocates it INSIDE the paper, framed by a border and a shadow, and drags "Put it back / Esc" 264px away from the column it belongs to while the foot rule spans 400px of nothing. Screenshot comparison at ?state=pressure is unambiguous: the current paper reads as a sheet on a desk, the "fixed" one reads as a mis-sized card with a paragraph in its left third. master.css line 269 names this exact failure as the thing that was fixed: "A 1262px card holding a 527px column is not a piece of paper on a desk, it is a big empty rectangle with a paragraph in the corner." The brief also lists "The desk paper is capped to its own content" as already landed. This finding proposes undoing a documented round-2 fix.

2. THE SECOND HALF OF THE FIX IS A NO-OP. `margin-inline: auto` on `.paperStack` changes nothing — `.paperStack` is already the full 1262px of the desk column; the paper is left-aligned inside it. Measured after applying it: `.top` still starts at l:130. The fix cannot "centre the desk over the index column" as written.

3. FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT THE FRAMES. "The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge" is false. Measured right edges at 1440: capture field 681, paper 846, hand card 816 inside a 846 hand top, peel 884 — the peel deliberately juts 38px past the paper's right edge, which is the whole visual gesture of a second sheet peeled off the note. Four different edges, staged.

4. "43% OF THE SHEET" IS INFLATED. The band is 43% of the desk row's WIDTH, not of the sheet. In the resting state the desk is 187px tall inside a 924px sheet, so the empty region is ~556x187 = 8.5% of the sheet, and the head above it and the pile below it both run the full width. The reader's eye crosses one short band, not an unfinished right half.

5. IT IS ALSO NOT "PERMANENTLY EMPTY IN EVERY STATE". In ?state=seam the 373px-tall peel occupies that vertical zone and overhangs the paper; in ?state=review the desk carries the hand; in ?state=voice the floor is ink.

The genuinely open question the finding brushes past is the opposite one: at 1920 the index rows stretch to 1882px while the paper holds at 716, so it is the INDEX that has no measure of its own, not the paper that is too narrow. That is a different finding with a different fix, and it is not what was filed.
